summary: Explores host configuration requirements for IPsec tunnel mode and describes how DHCPv4 can be used. In remote access, a host can be given a virtual address from the corporate network and its traffic tunneled, so it appears local. This document describes the DHCP mechanism for that.

plainLanguage.summary: When you connect to your office network from home, your computer needs an office-style address. This note explains how to hand one out using the usual address-giving service.

questions: how does dhcp work with ipsec tunnel mode
why use dhcp instead of ikecfg
subtitle: How a remote host gets a corporate address through an IPsec tunnel by reusing ordinary DHCPv4.

tldr.problem: A remote host that tunnels into a corporate network with IPsec tunnel mode needs an address and other settings from that network, so that it appears to be present locally.
tldr.mechanism: The host sets up a short-lived IPsec tunnel mode SA used only for DHCP, and runs a normal DHCPv4 exchange through it with the security gateway acting as a DHCP relay.
tldr.outcome: No new DHCP options and no changes to DHCPv4 or IKE are needed. The RFC concludes that DHCPv4 is the better choice than the IKECFG alternative.

today: RFC 3456 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It needs an htype value allocated in the arp-parameters registry and creates no new number spaces.

sections.title: Giving a Remote Host a Virtual Presence
sections.content:
In many remote access setups it is useful to make the remote host look as if it sits on the corporate network. The host gets a virtual address from the corporate network, and its traffic is tunneled with IPsec from its ISP-assigned address to the corporate security gateway.

RFC 3456 explores what host configuration needs in IPsec tunnel mode and describes how DHCPv4 (RFC 2131) can supply it. A DHCP client is a host using DHCP to get settings such as an address, and a DHCP server returns those settings.
sections.plainLanguage: Your laptop at home borrows an address from the office so the office network thinks it is sitting in the building. The office's normal address handout service does the lending.

sections.title: Why DHCP Fits the Requirements
sections.content:
Beyond the basic needs listed in RFC 3457 (an IPv4 address and other settings suited to the class of host), the RFC lists desirable extras: integration with existing address management, address pool management, reconfiguration, fail-over, simplicity and security in the IKE implementation, and authentication where required.

DHCPv4 covers these. The required parameters are a subset of the existing DHCPv4 options, so no new options and no changes to DHCPv4 are needed. Conditional behavior, for example through the User Class option, lets the gateway steer the host to the right address pool. Leases and a proposed forced reconfiguration handle reconfiguration. Because state lives on the DHCP server rather than inside IKE, losing a tunnel server does not lose that state, which eases fail-over. DHCPv4 authentication works on a tunnel interface as on any other.
sections.plainLanguage: The office already has a good system for handing out addresses and remembering who has which. Using it means nobody has to build a second system.

sections.title: The Configuration Walk-Through
sections.content:
The host already has Internet connectivity and knows where the security gateway is, which it can find through DNS using A, KX or SRV records. It ends up with two addresses: an Internet interface address used in the outer header of tunnel mode packets, and a virtual intranet interface address used in the inner header.

  • The host sets up an IKE security association with the gateway in main mode or aggressive mode.
  • It then sets up a DHCP SA in a quick mode exchange. This tunnel mode SA protects the first DHCP traffic and MUST only be used for DHCP.
  • DHCP messages flow between the host and the DHCPv4 server through that SA, and the intranet interface gets an address and other settings.
  • The host MAY delete the DHCP SA, or both sides MAY keep using it by adding temporary SPD selectors.
  • If a new tunnel is needed, the host sets up a tunnel mode SA by quick mode, and the newly assigned address SHOULD be used in the quick mode ID.

From then on all IP traffic, including later DHCPv4 messages, goes through the tunnel. The RFC notes the mechanism works best when the VPN uses a virtual interface.
sections.plainLanguage: First you build a small private pipe just for asking the office for an address. Once you have the address, you build the real pipe for everything else.

sections.title: The DHCPDISCOVER Message and Client Identity
sections.content:
The exchange starts with the intranet interface sending a DHCPDISCOVER. The htype field is set to 31, meaning an IPsec tunnel mode virtual interface, so the server can tell VPN requests from others. The broadcast bit MUST be zero, and giaddr carries the security gateway interface address.

The chaddr field MUST hold an identifier unique to the virtual subnet and the client MUST use the same value in the whole exchange. It SHOULD be persistent across reboots so the server can reassign the same address. It is normally taken from the active LAN interface with the lowest number. With no LAN interface, it SHOULD be built from x'4000', the IPv4 address of the connecting interface, and one more octet.

The client-identifier option MUST be included, MUST be unique within the virtual subnet and SHOULD be persistent. Options include the htype/chaddr pair, the machine FQDN plus an interface number, or the user NAI plus an interface number.
sections.plainLanguage: The request carries a special sticker saying it comes from a tunnel and a name tag that stays the same each time, so the office can hand you the same address again.

sections.title: The DHCP SA and the Security Gateway as Relay
sections.content:
The key lifetime of the DHCP SA SHOULD be on the order of minutes, since it is temporary. In the quick mode exchange the host SHOULD use an IDci payload of 0.0.0.0/UDP/port 68 and the gateway uses an IDcr payload of its own Internet address with UDP port 67. The filters are Any to Any with destination UDP port 67 from host to gateway, and destination UDP port 68 from gateway to host. The same SA also works for a host renewing a lease, in which case a DHCPREQUEST goes first. Both ends must handle the broadcast destination of the DHCPDISCOVER.

Typically the DHCP server is a separate machine and the gateway acts as a DHCP relay, putting its address in giaddr. It does not request or renew addresses for the client, and it MAY use relay load balancing. Relays are stateless, so the gateway SHOULD insert enough information to route the DHCPOFFER back to the right tunnel: either a separate subnet per tunnel with the interface address in giaddr, or the Relay Agent Information option (RFC 3046) with the tunnel's virtual port number in the Agent Circuit ID sub-option. The gateway usually snoops the yiaddr field in the DHCPACK to add a route to the client. If neither is possible, implementations MAY keep a mapping of xid, chaddr and tunnel, which the RFC calls undesirable for large VPN servers.

After the DHCPACK the host may delete the DHCP SA, and later DHCP messages travel through the newly established VPN SA. The host SHOULD be configurable to send all Internet-bound traffic through the tunnel, which adds overhead but lets the gateway filter it.
sections.plainLanguage: The office's front desk forwards your request to the address office and sends the answer back down the right pipe. After you have your address, the temporary pipe is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Limits and Policy
sections.content:
The DHCP packets between the host and the gateway are authenticated and integrity protected by IPsec. Between the gateway and the DHCP server there is no protection unless DHCP authentication is used.

Authenticated DHCP cannot work as an access control mechanism, because a remote host can set its own IP address. So the assigned address MUST NOT be relied on for security. The gateway can instead use packet filters or quick mode selectors per tunnel. Forwarding requests from untrusted sources raises DHCP exhaustion attacks and spoofing of the client identifier or MAC address, which the Relay Agent Information option can partly address.

For configuration policy, the server can look at the User Class option, htype/chaddr, host name, client-identifier, relay agent information, vendor class and vendor-specific options, or subnet selection. These give different configurations but, like the others, do not add security.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel keeps the request private on the way in, but a clever visitor can still pretend to have any address, so the office must check visitors in other ways.

sections.title: Why Not IKECFG
sections.content:
An appendix compares DHCPv4 with IKECFG (the ISAKMP Configuration Method, a work in progress at the time). It finds IKECFG does not meet the basic requirements. It supports an address and a few parameters such as DNS and WINS server addresses, but not DHCPv4's rich options. It is not integrated with existing address management, cannot let the host choose an address pool, has no leases or reconfiguration, and creates a separate pool of address state that complicates fail-over.

The RFC also warns that adding configuration, authentication and fail-over duplication to IKE would increase the scope of work and eventually compromise IKE security. It concludes that DHCPv4 is the superior alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: Building a second, smaller address system inside the tunnel software would be extra work and would be worse than the one everyone already uses.
